playbook:
**Playbook for ESTATE**

Buying is how I win. Final score is cash plus purchase price of deeds, so every dollar spent on a property converts 1:1 into score while also generating rent income. There is no penalty for being cash-poor except the inability to buy. When a property is unowned and I can afford it, I buy it — with one refinement below about pacing.

Buy aggressively early — but this game exposed the real cost of draining cash too fast. I bought Wharf (80) on lap 1 and Terrace (70) on lap 2, leaving myself at 68. Then I landed on Exchange (120) with 86 and Mill (90) with 86, and could buy neither. Those two misses cost me more than the early buys earned me: I finished with only two deeds while opponents picked up Foundry, Mill, and Depot behind me. So: buying to low cash is fine only if the remaining unowned tiles are cheap enough to buy out of salary and rent. When the board still holds expensive unowned tiles (Exchange at 120 especially), keep a buffer that can cover the next most expensive tile, or at least don't assume I can skip a mid-priced tile now and buy a big one later — the dice rarely cooperate.

Rough rule: if buying now leaves me with less than the price of the priciest remaining unowned tile, and that tile is one I could plausibly land on within two laps, consider holding one lap for salary + rent to accumulate. Cash shortage, not price selection, is the binding constraint. Rent owed to other investors drains me too — budget for landing on their tiles.

Prioritize by rent yield per price, but in a short game (6 laps) pure acquisition matters more than selection. Exchange (120/30) and Foundry (100/24) are the best tiles; missing Exchange was the biggest single loss this game. An expensive high-rent tile is worth taking if I can afford it — and worth saving up for.

I must track my true balance every turn. The prompt's "last declared balance" excludes receipts noted since my last turn ("you received N from other investors") and salary when passing START. Before declaring, I compute: last balance + rent received since last turn + salary if I passed START − rent I owe this turn − purchase price if buying. I did this correctly every turn this game; keep doing it explicitly each turn.

Also read the bank's transfer log: it tells me who owns what (via purchases) and whether rent was paid to me. Rent due to me may appear in the log before my turn — always include it. When rent is due to another investor, I pay it and subtract exactly that amount; nothing else changes hands.

Endgame: on the final lap, buying at face value is score-neutral in cash-plus-deed terms. Take the last-turn buy if affordable — at worst it's a wash. This game I had no buy available on lap 6 (Foundry owned, rent 24 paid) and finished at +255 = 105 cash + 150 in deeds.

Key failure to avoid: running my balance below the price of tiles still on the board. The lap-3/lap-4 lockout (86 vs 120 and 90) came directly from buying Terrace to near-zero on lap 2. Buy early and often, but keep enough cash that the next expensive unowned tile is still reachable.

1.text:
**Playbook for estate auction game**

When I land on an unowned property and have enough cash, buy it. The scoring formula is cash plus the purchase price of deeds held, so converting cash into a deed is score-neutral in the moment and strictly positive afterward: I gain the rent stream, deny opponents the tile, and a deed I own can never cost me rent. Judge extra value by rent-to-price ratio and location — a tile rivals hit often is worth snapping up first — but the default is buy.

The cash floor is much less important than I previously thought. In the last game I skipped a 120 tile on lap 3 because it would leave me with 2 cash; I ended the game with 33 cash and no Exchange, when buying it would have left roughly the same final score in cash terms plus the tile itself in the score — a large net gain. Since unspent cash counts 1:1 and deeds count 1:1 at purchase price, the only real cost of spending low is the risk of landing on an owned tile with nothing to pay. The maximum single rent here is 30. So the floor I need is not 50–60 — it's roughly one worst-case rent (30), and even that only matters if I haven't just passed START with salary coming. On the far side of the circuit, or with several laps left and salary due, buy down to near zero.

Put plainly: stretch for the expensive tiles when they come up. Passing on a big tile to "stay liquid" wastes the opportunity and gains nothing, because the cash I hoard scores the same 1:1 as the deed would — minus the rent income and denial I gave up.

Rent obligations are the only real danger of a low balance. If I'm down to a few coins, hope not to land on a rival's tile before the next salary. If I do land on one I can't fully cover, pay what I can and declare honestly — my own books are mine to keep, but accurate reporting is what the game asks of me.

When passing START, collect the salary first and include it in the declared balance. When a notice says I received money from other investors since my last turn, add it to my last declared balance before applying this turn's dues — forgetting this is an easy way to misreport.

Track opponents' purchases from the bank's transfer log. If rivals are hoarding the expensive tiles, the counter isn't staying liquid — it's outbidding them to whatever tile I land on before they do, since every tile they buy is rent I'll pay later and score they'll bank. The expensive tiles (Exchange at 120, Foundry at 100) are the biggest score swings: prioritize them whenever I land on them and can pay at all.

In the final lap, buy anything I land on, spending down to whatever remains after covering likely rent on the last few squares.

Keep the books exact: pay the bank for purchases, pay owners exactly for rent, and end every reply with the correct bracketed balance token.

2.text:
**Playbook for ESTATE**

Final wealth is declared cash plus purchase prices of deeds, so buying a property is a score-neutral cash conversion — money spent on purchase returns to my score immediately. Rent paid is pure loss; rent collected is pure gain. This means I should buy aggressively and early, as long as I keep enough cash to survive rent hits and to fund later purchases.

- When an unowned property is put to me and my post-purchase balance stays above roughly 20, I buy it. If buying would drop me near zero, I still buy unless I expect a large rent bill before my next salary — a cash cushion of 15–25 is only worth keeping if I'm likely to land on an owned high-rent tile before passing START.
- Prioritize purchases by rent-to-price ratio: Wharf (80/18), Foundry (100/24), Exchange (120/30), Mill (90/20) are the strong tiles; Depot (50/10) and Terrace (70/14) are middling. Given equal cash, take the better ratio first, since rental income compounds over the remaining laps.
- The biggest mistake this episode: buying Foundry for 100 dropped me to 82, which left me unable to buy Exchange (120) the very next turn. Before a purchase, check the prices of the *remaining unowned tiles*: if a 120 tile is still out, a post-purchase balance under 120 means I may be locked out of it. When two strong tiles remain, it's often better to buy the cheaper one and keep enough for the next opportunity — but never skip a strong tile purely to hoard, since skipping Foundry would have cost me both the deed and the 48 in rent it later collected.
- A purchase is score-neutral, but liquidity is not: it's the ability to buy the *next* tile that comes up. In this episode the sequence of rolls meant I hit two unowned tiles back to back; that's common on a small circuit, so the post-buy balance should be sized to the cheapest remaining unowned tile, not just a rent cushion.
- Late-game buys are still worth taking if affordable. I bought Depot for 50 on lap 4 of 6, leaving only 32 — but the purchase was score-neutral, denied it to opponents, and rent I collected afterwards was pure gain. Rent payback is a bonus, not the reason to buy; the reason is that deed price counts fully at the end. So buy even on the last laps if the balance after purchase won't bankrupt me before my next salary.
- Track other players' purchases from the bank's book: rent I owe depends on who owns what, and opponents who spent heavily early will be cash-poor — I can afford to spend down to a small cushion when they can't extract it. A player on a buying streak is likely to absorb the remaining tiles, which argues for buying sooner rather than holding out for better ratios.
- Always add any "received since last turn" rent to my last declared balance before computing payment and the new balance; forgetting inbound rent makes me understate my position. This episode inbound rent (48) arrived on the final turn and had to be folded into the closing balance.
- The [pay] token on a purchase goes to the bank, not another player; rent goes to the owner. Include the salary of 25 in the balance whenever I pass START.
- Track my position on the circuit: with an 8-tile loop and small rolls, landing on my own tiles is common in the endgame and nothing is due. On the final lap, with no purchase opportunities left worth taking, simply declare correctly and hoard. A final score of cash plus deed prices confirms that every affordable tile I took paid off at face value.
